 Best Portable Power Stations of 2026, Lab-Tested and Reviewed
 We tested models from Anker, EcoFlow, and Goal Zero, among others, to find the ones that will provide power the longest and recharge quickly
 By 
 Allen St. John 
 Senior Home & Tech Writer 
 By 
 Yasmeen Khan 
 Home & Garden Writer

 Updated September 2, 2026

 A portable power station can quietly keep your devices running, but you have to pause every now and then to recharge the battery.
 Photo: EcoFlow
 If you’ve ever used a pocket-sized power bank to recharge your phone, you’ll appreciate the utility of a portable power station . It’s essentially a large rechargeable lithium-ion battery with an array of outlets you can use to power appliances and other devices in your home and on the road.
 It can keep your gear running at a campsite or a tailgate party and, yes, during a power outage, too (though only for a limited stretch of time). Keep in mind that portable power stations won’t keep electric appliances and devices running for nearly as long as comparably sized generators , says Paolo Fu, who leads generator and portable power station testing for Consumer Reports. But power stations can be a great alternative to generators during short outages, of say, a couple of hours, or may last longer if you’re powering only a few key essentials at once.
 “Portable power stations can be handy during an outage to charge your phone, make emergency calls, stay in touch with loved ones, and keep a fridge or freezer running a little longer,” Fu says. “They are best for outages that last for hours, not days.”

 What to Eat During a Power Outage 
 Unlike a generator, a power station is sleek, quiet, and easy to use. It starts easily, without you having to worry about an engine that may have sat idle in the garage for months. It doesn’t saddle you with messy gasoline refills, clogged carburetors, or oil changes . Even more important, it eliminates the potentially deadly carbon monoxide fumes associated with generators.
 Before you rush out and buy one, though, consider the trade-offs. Power stations can be pricey and heavy, and the fastest way to recharge them is to plug them into an outlet, which is hard to do when the power’s out in your home. (You can slowly recharge them through their accompanying solar panels, and the solar panels can also extend the run time of your power station, but depending on the load, this may not be sufficient.)
 To help you weigh the pros and cons, we recently tested six popular models with their accompanying solar panels. They range in price from about $500 to more than $2,500. All have the capacity to provide backup power for key appliances in your home. They can also be quite large—ranging in size from a large car battery to a carry-on suitcase—and reasonably heavy, weighing 30 to nearly 100 pounds.
 For reviews of all the models we tested, check out our portable power station ratings and buying guide for more details.
 CR's Guide to Home Improvement
 Find  top-rated products and expert tips to help you save energy and money—and protect your home from extreme weather. 
 Best Portable Power Stations
 These are the best portable power stations from our tests, earning high marks for recharge speed, power delivery, power quality, portability, and ease of use. The prices (and our testing) include the power station plus its solar panels. The power stations can also be purchased separately, without the panels.
 What Can You Do With a Portable Power Station?
 The right-sized battery power station can deliver enough electricity to run essential systems and appliances, but only for a relatively short time. Smaller models can keep a laptop running and a few lights on, while much larger ones can be daisy-chained into a whole-house backup power solution.
 Your first task is to decide which devices and appliances you want to power and how much capacity you need to get the job done. Because a larger appliance like a refrigerator can kick on and off and cause a power surge, our experts recommend that you leave a little leeway between the total wattage of your appliances and the maximum power of your station. Energy Sage offers a guide on how much power appliances and other household electronics need.
 To help figure out what a portable power station can handle and for how long, take a look at the “claimed capacity” in watt hours (Wh) as well as the “claimed output” in watts in our ratings chart , Fu says. You’ll need to divide the power station’s capacity by its output to get a sense of how long the power station will run at full capacity.
 For example, the top model in our ratings, the EcoFlow Delta, has a claimed output of 3,600 watts and a claimed capacity of 3,600 watt-hours. If you want the EcoFlow working at full strength, delivering 3,600 watts to power all of the electronics you can—say, a refrigerator, laptop, television, five to 10 lights, and a medium window air conditioner—it would run for just one hour.
 If you want the EcoFlow to continuously power just your refrigerator, which draws about 700 watts, the power station would run for more than 5 hours on battery alone. (If you add the solar panel, it would extend the run time slightly, depending on solar conditions.) 
 A power station can also be used like an inverter generator to supply power at a campsite or a tailgate party. Indeed, power stations have become a staple on the road for those who revel in the adventures of van life . 
 They’re also a bit more flexible than generators at delivering power because they often supplement standard 120-volt, three-prong outlets with USB-A and USB-C ports for powering phones, laptops, and portable speakers.
 If you plan to take a portable power station on the road and use it outdoors, make sure you understand what kind of weather it can handle, Fu says. “Most solar panels we tested can handle any weather, but the power station itself may not be able to,” he says. “You don’t want to use the power station in the rain unless the manufacturer states that it’s waterproof.” 
 Or if you are using one in a dusty climate, make sure the manufacturer rates it for dust.
 Advantages of a Portable Power Station
 Here are the best reasons to invest in a portable power station:
 It’s quiet. Because it doesn’t have an engine, a portable power station is very quiet. Many don’t even have a cooling fan, so those—including the ones we’ve tested—are dead silent. (If your power station doesn’t have a cooling fan, Fu says to make sure to monitor it in the heat.) While tranquility may not be a huge consideration when your electricity is out, a near-silent power source at a campsite allows you to hear the lilting birdsong of a wood thrush instead of the rumble of a generator.
 It doesn’t emit dangerous carbon monoxide fumes. As a result, portable power stations don’t require the safety precautions of a generator, which include outdoor placement at least 20 feet from a home or garage, with the exhaust directed away from windows, doors, and air conditioners. You can run a power station in your kitchen, basement, or garage, so you don’t need an awning to keep the unit dry, as you would with a generator. That makes a power station a compelling alternative for apartment dwellers who want emergency backup power but lack the outdoor space to run a generator.
 It has excellent power quality. All of the power stations we’ve tested earn top marks for power quality, which is the ability to deliver clean power without the dips and spikes that can damage sensitive electronics. Their power quality is higher than most standard (noninverter) generators we’ve tested.
 Disadvantages of a Portable Power Station
 Here are the reasons you might choose to avoid a portable power station:
 It isn’t always convenient. The biggest disadvantage is that, like any battery, your power station will run out of power. And when that happens, you have to disconnect the unit and recharge it—a process that can take hours. That’s an inconvenience if you’re using the power station to charge your laptop, but it’s a major problem if you’re relying on it to keep food cold or power vital medical equipment. A generator has a big advantage here. Yes, it can run out of fuel, but when that happens, you just turn it off and refill the tank from a gas can, with only the briefest interruption of power.
 Its recharge rate can be slow. Not all portable power stations recharge at the same rate. When calculating Overall Scores, our testers assign the highest weight to recharge speed. Each of the models we’ve tested has portable solar panels that can recharge it, but the process is often slow, especially when the sky is overcast. You’re better off using the panels to extend the battery’s range, not to recharge it. And just as the power stations recharge at different rates, they deplete at different rates, too. Some are more efficient than others when powering the same load and can last longer.
 It’s heavy. And, for what it’s worth, portable power stations are not always easy to transport. Some heavier models come with wheels, like the 97-pound EcoFlow Delta Pro. But other models in our ratings don’t. CR evaluates handles as part of the portability rating because even lighter models—ranging from 30 to 60 pounds—should have one that’s easy to grip.
 It’s expensive. Finally, portable power stations are quite expensive. Our top-rated model—the EcoFlow Delta Pro—puts out 3,600 watts and costs more than $2,500. For comparison, you can buy a highly rated 3,900-watt inverter generator like the Generac iQ5200DF for about $1,000.
 Should You Buy a Portable Power Station?
 It ultimately comes down to how you plan to use it.
 Our ratings chart can help you zero in on a model that delivers high-quality power. But for many people, a gas-powered generator will be cheaper and more effective in a lengthy power outage, such as after a storm or other natural disaster.
 But if a portable power station’s most important virtues—quiet operation and the placement flexibility that comes with a lack of dangerous emissions—suit your needs, you might find it worthwhile to pay more than you would for a comparably sized generator.
 How CR Tests Portable Power Stations
 In our labs, CR test engineers evaluate five key measures to rate portable power stations: recharge speed, power delivery, power quality, portability, and ease of use. We don’t test the manufacturer’s run time claims, nor do we include noise evaluations in our ratings, because we found that, as a category, portable power stations run silently. 
 Recharge speed is based on how quickly the station charges while plugged into a 120-volt power source and while using the power station’s accompanying solar panels.
 Power delivery is based on how well the voltage is maintained and how well the unit handles surges in power. Higher power output means more equipment can be run simultaneously. Power quality reflects the station’s ability to deliver clean power over various loads. 
 To assess portability, we evaluate the power station’s ergonomics. To assess ease of use, we evaluate features including the number of outlets, USB port outputs, whether the power station has clear indicators of remaining power, and whether it comes with a companion app.
 Allen St. John
 Allen St. John has been a senior product editor at CR since 2016, focusing on digital privacy, audio devices, printers, and home products. He was a senior editor at Condé Nast and a contributing editor at publications including Road & Track and The Village Voice. A New York Times bestselling author, he's also written for The New York Times Magazine, The Wall Street Journal, and Rolling Stone. He lives in Montclair, N.J., with his wife, their two children, and their dog, Rugby.

 Yasmeen Khan is a multimedia content creator at Consumer Reports. She covers topics related to home systems and tools, like lawn mowers and generators. Before joining CR, Yasmeen was a longtime news reporter for WNYC in New York City. She has also worked as a story editor and host of podcasts.

 Power stations are ideal for helping you get through a power outage and for off-grid camping. They offer a compelling alternative to loud and smelly generators. And, unlike gas generators, power stations don't emit potentially lethal carbon monoxide fumes and can be recharged with optional solar panels . 
 The Jackery 2000 v2 is the best power station for those who need additional power for multi-day off-grid camping, or for an extended blackout. Recently reduced in price, it can now be found for under $900 on Amazon. At 39 lbs, it is light enough that most people will find it easy to pack and move around, and it is easy to add optional solar recharging. It's our favorite option for extended off-grid camping.
 The best value power station for most people is the Anker C1000 Gen 2 . It delivers on most people's basic needs, such as getting through a blackout in comfort, providing power for an off-grid camping trip, or offering portable power away from a 110V outlet. Affordably priced — currently on sale for under $530 — it offers a combination of price, power, and portability that hits the sweet spot: ample power without breaking the bank. 
 If your primary goal is home backup power, step up to the EcoFlow Delta Pro 3 . It is designed specifically for home backup power use, and can be wired directly into your home breaker panel with an optional transfer switch kit. It has an impressive 4.0 kWh power capacity, which can be expanded to up to 48 kWh. 
 After considering more than 40 models, we purchased and tested today's top 14 power stations. Our extensive side-by-side tests measured the runtime delivered with everything from home appliances to camping gear. We also measured the number of recharges you can deliver to an iPhone, a laptop, or a cordless drill.

 The Jackery Explorer 2000 v2 offers ample power to support multi-day off-grid camping needs and allow you to stay comfortable during an extended blackout. It delivers quiet operation and is relatively easy to tote around at 39 lbs. It offers an impressive 2,042 Wh capacity, of which we measured 1,710 Wh available as usable AC power output. The 2000 v2 provides fast-charging capabilities, reaching 100% in 2.5 hours through AC input. It offers easy-to-use solar panel support, ideal for handling extended off-grid camping or sustained power outages. Paired with (1) or (2) 200 watt solar panels, it is easy to recharge the 2000 v2 on sunny days. One tester noted, “ The Jackery 2000 v2 is my go-to for camping. Small and light enough to be easy to use, it offers plenty of power for a cool campsite with string lights, an electric cooler, and recharging devices .”
 One drawback of the Jackery 2000 v2 is the lack of an expandable battery capacity option. We don't consider that a deal breaker, since you can simply buy another one if you need more power down the road. While it provides plenty of power for off-grid camping needs or for powering lights or tools wherever you need them, the v2 does not offer sufficient runtime for multi-day cooking on an electric burner or for running a space heater (less than 2 hours of runtime). And, if you need to fully recharge an e-bike, that will drain more than half of the v2's capacity. Solar panels are an easy-to-use option to extend the v2's capacity, and Jackery solar panels are well-made and extremely easy to use. For those with existing non-Jackery-branded solar panels, buying an adapter cable is required (about $25 on Amazon).  The EcoFlow Delta Pro 3 is a large, high-capacity power station designed for home backup power. Its 4,000-watt output and 4,096 Wh capacity allow for high-wattage appliance use and extended blackout capability. With expansion options up to 48 kWh, the Delta Pro 3 is a great starting point for those looking to transition to full home backup power. It also supports up to 2,600 watts of solar charging, allowing you to utilize solar in van builds and off-grid home use. EcoFlow makes an optional Transfer Switch Kit that makes it easy and fast to use the Delta Pro 3 to power your essential home circuits during a blackout. As our tester notes, “ the Delta Pro 3's ample power and battery expansion potential made it my go-to choice to build out my home backup setup .”
 ​The biggest downside to the EcoFlow Delta Pro 3 is its weight. At 114.1 lbs, it's better suited to a semi-permanent location inside your garage than it is on a camping trip. Despite its sturdy wheels and telescoping handle, the sheer size and weight of this unit make moving it difficult, if not impractical, with its wheels only cooperating on smooth, even terrain. It's also one of the most expensive power stations on the market, with a relatively poor price to capacity of $0.90/Wh. Despite its heavy weight and hefty price tag, we wouldn't hesitate to recommend the Delta Pro 3 for those with large power needs and home backup in mind.

 How We Tested
 Our testing process for power stations is extensive. We subject each product to hundreds of hours of hands-on use and testing to evaluate power output, runtime, device compatibility, and ease of operation. 
 We do not rely on manufacturer claims or specifications to determine things like each product's actual usable AC power output. We use sophisticated power measurement equipment, along with some creative test jigs of our own custom design, to stress test each product and measure its real-world capabilities. 
 None of the products we tested actually delivers usable AC power output that matches their claimed capacity . For example, a 2,000 watt-hour power station will not provide you with 2,000 watt-hours of usable AC power — only 60% to 93% of the claimed capacity is actually delivered and usable to power your devices through the AC outlets. Since products vary so widely in the actual usable power they deliver, we consider the usable AC power output to be the single most important information to help guide your purchase decision-making. 
 We use precision power measurement equipment to measure runtime and charging speeds. You can learn more about our power station testing protocol and process, in our How We Test article. 
Our tests inform our rating scores, which reflect the four key factors we believe are most important for you to make a smarter purchase decision:
 Power Output (60% of overall score weighting) 
 Portability (25% weighting) 
 Charge Speed (10% weighting) 
 Features (5% weighting)

 Why Trust GearLab
 Our power station test team have a combined 20 years of experience using power stations in conditions ranging from power outages to off-grid camping to remote tool use. Our review team includes experts in electronics, off-grid power and solar charging, and consumer-electronics review and testing. 
 GearLab co-founder RJ Spurrier , a Robotics Engineer educated at UC Berkeley's Engineering school, has been using power stations for more than 15 years, starting from the time he organized an off-grid movie night with friends on San Francisco's Ocean Beach. Today, RJ is a dedicated off-grid camper with his family, using solar panels and power stations to enable extended outdoor adventures across the mountains and deserts of the US West. RJ also uses power station batteries and solar panels to power his net-zero home , which combines a 45-panel solar array with a 20 kWh power station system for home backup.
 Senior Research Analyst, Sentry Kelly boasts a formal education in Applied Manufacturing Engineering, Sentry has the knowledge and training to analyze just about any mechanical or electrical product out there. In his free time, Sentry and his wife travel far and wide in his custom-built van that is outfitted with solar panels and a power station as the primary power source for their extended off-grid camping adventures. 
 Research Analyst Kenji Mowrey leads our field testing of each power station. Kenji earned his bachelor's degree in Outdoor Product Design from Oregon State and has a lifelong passion and curiosity for discovering what separates good consumer products from the great ones. Kenji blends his analytical and science-based testing with a pursuit of electronics and outdoor equipment that are simply a joy to use, never let you down, and work just as expected. 
 Analysis and Test Results
 In the following section, we share our findings from our extensive testing of each competing product.

 What's the Best Value?
 The Jackery 300 is the winner of our Best Buy award because it is small, affordable, and a great solution for keeping your phone and laptop recharged. However, it won't be a great value if your goal is to power higher-wattage devices or appliances — for example, you can't power a space heater, stove burner, or even a hot water kettle with the Jackery 300. 
 Figure out how much power you need . From our perspective, the best value strategy for power stations is to focus on what you want to power and avoid overspending on more capacity than you actually need. 
 Choosing the right power station is largely determined by your power needs. To save money, first figure out how much power you need, then pick the best device that meets your needs.   Credit: Matt Lighthart 
 While it is tempting to jump to higher power output, keep in mind that doubling power capacity will double the cost (and the weight). It might not be worth it. (Although we admittedly find ourselves wanting more power now for off-grid camping than we did in the past.)
 Adding Solar Can Save You Money 
A 2,000 Wh power station like the Jackery 2000 v2 might be all the power you need for a weekend camping trip. But you are unlikely to get 5-7 days of off-grid camping power out of it. Going to a 4,000 Wh power station could solve that problem, but it will cost you another $1,000 . A more economical solution? Consider adding a 200 watt solar panel for less than $400 , which might extend your runtime for days.
 The good news is costs are coming down . Unlike most consumer electronics categories, power stations and solar panels have become much more affordable over the last few years. In 2024, each 1,000 Wh of power station capacity would cost you about $1,000, or $1/Wh. Today, many of the most compelling power station products can be found for less than half that cost — around $0.40/Wh.

 How to Choose A Power Station
 Before deciding which power station will be right for you, there are a few key factors to consider. Below are some key questions that summarize key points from our buying advice article.
 An electric cooler is very convenient for camping. But, be sure to bring it to a cool temperature at home or when plugged into your car 12v plug while driving, since the initial cooling is when it draws the most power.   Credit: Matt Lighthart 
 How Much Power Do I Need? 
 Power stations are more limited in the maximum AC wattage and runtime they can provide, which is intuitively obvious. We are all accustomed to plugging in whatever we want into an AC outlet, and it just works. But, off-grid camping power or managing through a multi-day blackout requires planning about what kinds of devices you run to avoid fully depleting your power station prematurely. Dialing in your power station requirements takes discipline: you may need to pull back from what you want , to think about what you really need . 
 The Power Output section above includes some tables to help you determine what power station capacity will best meet your requirements.
 Note that certain kinds of devices, like space heaters, cooking appliances, and charging ebikes, are much more demanding of power than most other common devices. If you desire to run these higher-power devices, you'll want to calculate your power needs more carefully to ensure you have capacity for the runtime you need. 
 For multi-day power needs, adding optional solar panels may be helpful. Read on below for more info on solar panels.
One of our Editors has invested in a large-scale solar panel system for his home, with 45 solar panels on his roof, and an integrated power station battery capacity of 20 kWh. He notes, “ Our home puts more power into the grid each year than we use, and the power station batteries allow us to pull power when needed during lower-rate cost times of the day. And, we push power onto the grid in the summer during the highest rate for reimbursement times of day. ” Yet, even with that large-scale home backup system, it does not provide enough power for a 24-hour power outage during winter unless he turns off the breakers for all non-essential circuits. The reality is that providing the daily power most on-grid homeowners are accustomed to is beyond the capability of most solar + power station systems.
 What's Your Favorite Electric Gear for Off-grid Camping? 
 We are unabashed fans of electric camping . It can take a yeoman camping trip in the middle of nowhere and turn it into a magical romantic experience or a family fun adventure everyone will remember for years to come. Here's a list of some of our favorite gear and their power requirements:
 LED String Lights — ok, we've got to start with this, because whether it is romance, or a magical family experience, it is all about the lighting . For less than $20 for our best buy winner in string lights , which consumes less than 30 watts of power, you can dress up your campsite with 25 warm glowing LED lights. Oooh. So nice. We love it! And, learn how to play guitar too (acoustic, please) for the full monte. 
 Electric Cooler — we started reviewing electric coolers years ago, but only recently have they become truly awesome. Skip that stop at the store to buy ice, skip all the space taken by the ice, and eliminate the yucky pool of melted water getting in your food on Sunday morning — welcome to the new core tool for camping: the electric cooler. It is a game changer. Pro tip: extend your power station runtime by cooling down your electric cooler using AC power at home, or on the drive plugged into your car 12v plug --it is when cooling down that a powered cooler requires the most electricity. 
 Outdoor Projector — yeah, that is a thing too. Family camping experience: check! Remote location: check! Pixar movie at your campsite: coolest parents ever ! But, do have your power station handy and not fully drained. A quality outdoor projector like the XGIMI Halo+ is a great choice and has its own battery, but if that battery runs out 10 mins before the movie ends, you will go from coolest parents ever to a total meltdown — the power station might save the day (and let you watch more than one movie too)! 
 LED Lanterns — while there may be some who have nostalgia for old-school kerosene or white gas mantel lanterns, at GearLab we love modern LED Lanterns for safe and quiet task lighting when preparing meals. Even if you have a full set of LED String lights, it is great to have a bright rechargeable LED Lantern (or two) when preparing meals or putting a band-aid on a kiddo. 
 Induction Electric Burner — not everyone is ready to give up their old-school fuel-based Coleman camping stove, but we think they are going away in the future too. The full electric camping experience embraces an induction burner (1800W) to replace old-school propane and white gas camping stoves (note you'll need induction-compatible pots and pans to go with it). An induction burner is safer when camping with kids, more efficient with power usage than an old-school electric burner, and you'll rid yourself of the fuel, the fumes, and the fire risks associated with an old-school fuel camping stove . 
 Electric Kettle — boiling water is a recurring task when camping, whether it's for coffee, tea, oatmeal, hot chocolate, or instant “ just-add-water ” foods. A basic electric kettle (1500W) just makes it so easy and fast. 
 Electric Griddle — Another slick addition to your electric camping dream set-up is an electric griddle (1500W). They are great for cooking pancakes, eggs, grilled cheese sandwiches, bacon, sausage links, and more. 
Keep in mind the power you'll need, which adds up fast. You'll want at least a 2,000 Wh power station, and one with at least 2,000 AC watt support. The cooking devices are high AC Watt so you'll need to run them one at a time unless you buy a higher capacity power station. We love having all three — a kettle , an induction burner , and a griddle — but if space is tight, a burner alone will do. Adding one or two 200 watt solar panels will greatly extend your battery runtime by recharging your power station on sunny days.
 Are Solar Panel(s) a Must-have for a Power Station? 
 No. Many people do not need to invest in solar panels for their power station . The only reason to consider a solar panel is if you need more power over multiple days than your power station can provide. For most people, a suitable power station, like the Jackery 2000 v2 will provide you with adequate power for comfort during a multi-hour blackout and/or a typical weekend camping trip. Obtaining a 12v car adapter charging cable for your power station is a low-cost way to recharge anytime you use your vehicle when camping. 
 In our experience, it is when you need support for 3 or more days without grid power that a solar panel becomes a necessity. 
 A 3-day weekend off-grid camping trip can easily drain your power station and leave you with no power halfway into your trip. 
For example, we recently did a 3-day family camping trip in the Sierra Nevada mountain range using the Jackery 2000 v2. Our off-grid campsite included amenities such as LED string lights, an electric cooler, an inductive stove, two ebikes, recharging phones and iPads, and a SpaceX Starlink system. That camp setup draws too much power each day to make it through a 3-day trip. But, by using two 200 watt solar panels, we were able to fully charge up each day. One tester said, “ It was liberating to camp off-grid, in the middle of nowhere, and with such a cool camp setup. My family had a blast! In fact, we had plenty of power to be out there for a week or more of off-grid camping, so long as the sun kept shining .”

If that is insufficient, consider adding a second 200-watt panel, which will meet the needs of most people for extended off-grid camping or power blackouts.

A fully integrated solar + battery power solution will require that you obtain a permit from your electrical utility provider so you can sell excess your solar electricity to your power company and draw power from the grid during lower-cost times of day. This class of integrated solar + battery power solutions can deliver significant long-term economic benefits as well as qualify for tax incentives. But, they are not DIY solutions, and you'll need the help of an authorized installer and electrician to put it all together and obtain the necessary permits. If you are interested in this class of solution, we encourage you to solicit competitive bids from reputable solar installers in your area to get a better sense of your options before making a big investment in something like Ecoflow's Ultra X. 
 Bluetti Elite 30 V2 — The Elite 30 V2 is a small form power station intended for device charging and small appliance use. It offers 288 Wh and weighs 9.5 lbs. It works well for small tasks like charging devices and running small appliances, but there are more compelling options in the 200-300 Wh class. 
 Jackery Explorer 5000 Plus — The 5000 Plus sports a 5040 Wh capacity, ideal for powering large home appliances during blackouts, with 240V outlet configurations and expansion options capable of supplying multiple days of backup power. A power station this size is a significant investment and is most practical when integrated with your home's circuits via a transfer switch kit, along with solar panels and additional battery packs, which quickly increases the cost and benefit of owning a power station over a gas generator. 
 Jackery Explorer 500 — The Jackery Explorer 500 shares many of the same qualities as the smaller Jackery 300 but with a bigger battery capacity and higher power output. Though it takes over 5 hours to recharge via a standard wall outlet and has only a single AC port, making it less practical for anything beyond charging phones and laptops. 
 Goal Zero Yeti 500 — The Yeti 500 is a 499 Wh power station that weighs 16 lbs and produces 500 watts of power output. The Yeti 500 has enough power to run some appliances, such as a CPAP machine, but is underpowered for larger items like coffee makers and induction cooktops. Given the limited ports, like only having 2 AC outlets and just one 60 watt USb-C port, there are more enticing options available in the 500 Wh category. 
 DJI Power 2000 — The Power 2000 is DJI's debut in the power station market. It's large enough to cover multiple days of camping or keep an appliance or two charged during an outage. It has a couple of enticing features, such as a 30A RV plug and eight USB-C/USB-A ports. However, the proprietary charging ports are disappointing; you'll need to purchase additional accessories for solar or car charging, quickly making the 2000 an expensive option, especially compared to almost every competitor that has built-in solar and car charging ports. 
 EcoFlow Delta 3 Max — The Delta 3 Max is a beefed up version of the popular EcoFlow Delta 3 . It has double the battery capacity at 2048 Wh and a power output of 2400 watts. The tradeoff is that it weighs 44 lbs and costs a few hundred dollars more than the Delta 3. If you like the Delta lineup but need a bit more capability and battery storage, the Delta 3 Max is worth considering. 
 Anker Solix F3800 — The F3800 is a large, home backup power station that serves as a starting point for building out a full-scale home backup system. It has expandability up to 53.8 kWh, enough to power your home for multiple days during outages. The dual 120V/240V outlet opens up more appliance options, such as clothes dryers and electric ranges, and it also directly supports EV charging via the NEMA 14-50 port. Like any other large, home backup power station, the F3800 is a significant investment and is difficult to transport or move. 
 Conclusion
 Our breakdown of portable power stations aims to simplify the confusing and continually evolving information involved in purchasing one. After months of extensive testing and research, we hope our portable power station review provides the necessary knowledge and guidance to help you make an informed decision about your power needs.

For this guide, our experts conducted a detailed technical review of over 30 solar generators , then performed hands-on testing of the top dozen models, both in our Lab and in the homes of a dozen consumer testers over the course of several months. Our evaluations focused on the following: Good Housekeeping/Philip Friedman ✔️ Charge time and capacity Verified claimed charging times using solar panels and AC wall outlets in our Lab. Tested claimed capacity by running electronic devices with corresponding energy loads (e.g., 1,500-watt heaters for large-capacity, laptops for small-capacity) in our Lab. Consumer testers measured solar charge times and capacity under real-world conditions at home. Our engineers reviewed technical data to confirm shelf life (how long charge is held) and life cycle (number of recharges). ✔️ Usability Checked total number of outlets to gauge how many devices can be charged simultaneously. Assessed user-friendly features such as carrying handles, wheels, LED lights, and onboard storage. ✔️ Durability Tested durability of both the generator and solar panels for long-term performance. Advertisement - Continue Reading Below What to look for when shopping for solar-powered generators Solar generators come in various shapes and sizes to meet different needs. Key factors to consider include: ✔️ Capacity The more watts, the more power a generator can deliver, so consider your home’s power needs. Small generators have capacities around 250 watts, while larger ones offer 3,000 watts or more. Overloading a generator can damage it and connected electronics. Also consider run time: To power a 200-watt refrigerator for 10 hours, you'll need a 2,000-watt generator. For an eight-hour run of a 40-watt CPAP machine, a 500-watt generator is sufficient. ✔️ Solar panel compatibility Solar panel capacity affects charging speed. Our experts recommend at least 100-watt solar panels, and daisy-chaining multiple panels can speed up charging. Generators can charge via wall outlets, but solar panels are the fastest. ✔️ Battery type There are three main battery types—lithium ion, LiFePO4, and solid-state—each with pros and cons. Lithium-ion batteries are most common, offering safe, reliable power and have been the standard for solar generators for years. LiFePO4 batteries are the latest technology, providing longer lifespans and faster charging, though they struggle in extremely cold temperatures. Solid-state batteries are emerging and rely on solid electrolytes rather than the liquid electrolyte solution found in lithium batteries. They offer higher capacities but tend to be bulkier and heavier. ✔️ Portability Weight, which can range from 10 to over 100 pounds, often correlates with capacity. If you need to take your generator on the go, look for user-friendly features like wheels and telescoping handles for easier transport. Solar panels can also be heavy, so handles and carrying cases improve portability. How do I decide between a solar vs. a gas generator? Good Housekeeping/Jillian Sollazzo Gas backup generators were once the go-to for power outages, but our experts recommend considering solar-powered options. While gas generators are effective, they're noisy, fuel-hungry, and must be used outdoors to avoid harmful fumes. In contrast, solar-powered generators are emissions-free, safe for indoor use, and much quieter, ensuring they won't disrupt your household while keeping everything running. When deciding between a solar and gas generator, consider your power needs and budget. For lower power needs under 3,000 watts, solar generators are ideal, while gas generators work better for larger demands, especially 10,000 watts or more. If automatic backup power is essential, a standby gas generator is reliable and easier to install, although some solar options offer this with more complex setups. Solar generators are safer as they produce no emissions, making them suitable for indoor use, while gas generators can pose potential carbon monoxide risks. Read more in our guide to solar vs. gas generators . Advertisement - Continue Reading Below How do solar-powered generators work? A solar generator is essentially a large rechargeable battery that powers electronic devices. The fastest way to charge it is by plugging it into a wall outlet, similar to charging a phone or computer. However, solar generators can also be charged using solar panels, making them invaluable during extended power outages when plug-in charging isn’t an option. What size solar panels do I need? Large whole-house generators can be integrated with rooftop solar panels , functioning similarly to a battery backup system like the Tesla Powerwall, storing energy until it's needed. Solar generators of all sizes can also be charged with portable solar panels, which connect to the battery via a standard solar cable. These panels typically range from 100 to 400 watts and can be daisy-chained for faster charging. Depending on conditions, a solar generator may be fully charged by the sun in as little as four hours, though it can take up to 10 hours or longer. Therefore, it's essential to plan ahead, especially when extreme weather is on the horizon. Advertisement - Continue Reading Below Why are solar-powered generators also called portable power stations? Since this is still an emerging category, the industry is still figuring some things out—including what to call this new type of generator. It's also worth noting that the market for solar-powered generators is now splitting into "portable" and "whole-house" categories, similar to how gas generators come in either portable or standby models. Comparatively, whole-house power stations, while heavy (100+ pounds), are technically portable since they can be moved, unlike standby generators. However, consumers are unlikely to haul one outside to charge via solar power. Why trust Good Housekeeping? Dan DiClerico has covered the residential energy market for 25 years, focusing on energy-efficient solutions for the home, as well as emerging alternative technologies. As the director of the Home Improvement & Outdoor Lab at the Good Housekeeping Institute, DiClerico oversees solar generator testing with our engineers, product analysts, and consumer testers. He regularly attends trade shows to stay current on industry innovations and to speak on housing and home improvement topics. For this guide, our experts conducted a detailed technical review of over 30 solar generators , then performed hands-on testing of the top dozen models, both in our Lab and in the homes of a dozen consumer testers over the course of several months. Our evaluations focused on the following: Good Housekeeping/Philip Friedman ✔️ Charge time and capacity Verified claimed charging times using solar panels and AC wall outlets in our Lab. Tested claimed capacity by running electronic devices with corresponding energy loads (e.g., 1,500-watt heaters for large-capacity, laptops for small-capacity) in our Lab. Consumer testers measured solar charge times and capacity under real-world conditions at home. Our engineers reviewed technical data to confirm shelf life (how long charge is held) and life cycle (number of recharges). ✔️ Usability Checked total number of outlets to gauge how many devices can be charged simultaneously. Assessed user-friendly features such as carrying handles, wheels, LED lights, and onboard storage. ✔️ Durability Tested durability of both the generator and solar panels for long-term performance. Advertisement - Continue Reading Below What to look for when shopping for solar-powered generators Solar generators come in various shapes and sizes to meet different needs. Key factors to consider include: ✔️ Capacity The more watts, the more power a generator can deliver, so consider your home’s power needs. Small generators have capacities around 250 watts, while larger ones offer 3,000 watts or more. Overloading a generator can damage it and connected electronics. Also consider run time: To power a 200-watt refrigerator for 10 hours, you'll need a 2,000-watt generator. For an eight-hour run of a 40-watt CPAP machine, a 500-watt generator is sufficient. ✔️ Solar panel compatibility Solar panel capacity affects charging speed. Our experts recommend at least 100-watt solar panels, and daisy-chaining multiple panels can speed up charging. Generators can charge via wall outlets, but solar panels are the fastest. ✔️ Battery type There are three main battery types—lithium ion, LiFePO4, and solid-state—each with pros and cons. Lithium-ion batteries are most common, offering safe, reliable power and have been the standard for solar generators for years. LiFePO4 batteries are the latest technology, providing longer lifespans and faster charging, though they struggle in extremely cold temperatures. Solid-state batteries are emerging and rely on solid electrolytes rather than the liquid electrolyte solution found in lithium batteries. They offer higher capacities but tend to be bulkier and heavier. ✔️ Portability Weight, which can range from 10 to over 100 pounds, often correlates with capacity. If you need to take your generator on the go, look for user-friendly features like wheels and telescoping handles for easier transport. Solar panels can also be heavy, so handles and carrying cases improve portability. How do I decide between a solar vs. a gas generator? Good Housekeeping/Jillian Sollazzo Gas backup generators were once the go-to for power outages, but our experts recommend considering solar-powered options. While gas generators are effective, they're noisy, fuel-hungry, and must be used outdoors to avoid harmful fumes. In contrast, solar-powered generators are emissions-free, safe for indoor use, and much quieter, ensuring they won't disrupt your household while keeping everything running. When deciding between a solar and gas generator, consider your power needs and budget. For lower power needs under 3,000 watts, solar generators are ideal, while gas generators work better for larger demands, especially 10,000 watts or more. If automatic backup power is essential, a standby gas generator is reliable and easier to install, although some solar options offer this with more complex setups. Solar generators are safer as they produce no emissions, making them suitable for indoor use, while gas generators can pose potential carbon monoxide risks. Read more in our guide to solar vs. gas generators . Advertisement - Continue Reading Below How do solar-powered generators work? A solar generator is essentially a large rechargeable battery that powers electronic devices. The fastest way to charge it is by plugging it into a wall outlet, similar to charging a phone or computer. However, solar generators can also be charged using solar panels, making them invaluable during extended power outages when plug-in charging isn’t an option. What size solar panels do I need? Large whole-house generators can be integrated with rooftop solar panels , functioning similarly to a battery backup system like the Tesla Powerwall, storing energy until it's needed. Solar generators of all sizes can also be charged with portable solar panels, which connect to the battery via a standard solar cable. These panels typically range from 100 to 400 watts and can be daisy-chained for faster charging. Depending on conditions, a solar generator may be fully charged by the sun in as little as four hours, though it can take up to 10 hours or longer. Therefore, it's essential to plan ahead, especially when extreme weather is on the horizon. Advertisement - Continue Reading Below Why are solar-powered generators also called portable power stations? Since this is still an emerging category, the industry is still figuring some things out—including what to call this new type of generator. It's also worth noting that the market for solar-powered generators is now splitting into "portable" and "whole-house" categories, similar to how gas generators come in either portable or standby models. Comparatively, whole-house power stations, while heavy (100+ pounds), are technically portable since they can be moved, unlike standby generators. However, consumers are unlikely to haul one outside to charge via solar power. Why trust Good Housekeeping? Hurricane Helene

Hurricane Helene (September 2024) remains the largest event PowerOutage.us tracked in 2024, with 4.79 million customers affected. Western North Carolina's mountain communities faced outages exceeding 14 days. This was a scenario where a mid-size 2,000 Wh station would have been exhausted within two days of moderate use, and only a high-capacity unit with solar recharging could sustain emergency household energy through the full duration.

Hurricane Milton

Hurricane Milton (October 2024) revealed a different challenge: cycling grid failures, with power coming on and off for brief windows of 30 minutes to two hours. That pattern put a premium on fast-charging solar generators that could top off batteries during those windows. For example, the advantages that units like the Goal Zero Yeti PRO 4000 and EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3 hold over slower-charging alternatives.

Overall, these events show households can make use of solar generators with enough capacity to last multiple days and enough solar input to keep recharging without relying on the grid.

Benefits of solar generators vs. gas generators

Solar portable generators have a number of distinct advantages for partial home backup and recreational use. Some notable benefits include:

Clean, renewable energy source with zero emissions
Free energy generation from solar power
No need to store flammable, unstable fuel
Fewer maintenance needs than combustible engine generators
Safer to operate as an emergency backup energy source in homes
Can also be charged from grid power through your home electrical system
Silent operation for annoyance-free nighttime or indoor use

Note that while solar portable generators are safer to use in homes due to the absence of emissions and combustible fuel, it is still important to follow basic generator safety precautions. Refer to your solar generator's user manual for safe operating guidelines. Whole-home backup claims also assume load management, compatible transfer equipment, and in many cases multiple battery units.

Note that a solar generator doesn't technically generate electricity, it stores it. You charge it either by connecting solar panels or plugging into a wall outlet, then draw on that stored energy when you need it. Without a recharge source, a fully depleted unit simply won't power anything until it's recharged.

What to look for in a solar portable generator

Solar generators come with long lists of technical specifications, but some are more relevant for usability than others. Here are the key features worth focusing on.

Battery specifications
Type: Lithium-ion batteries have become the industry standard over traditional lead-acid deep-cycle batteries, due to their superior capacity and faster charging. LFP (LiFePO₄) chemistry offers particularly strong cycle life and is used by several units on our list.
Capacity: Typically measured in watt-hours or kilowatt-hours, capacity represents the maximum amount of energy a battery can hold in reserve.
Cycle life: The total number of times a battery can be fully depleted and recharged before capacity degrades meaningfully.
Inverter type

Pure sine wave inverters are more efficient than modified sine wave alternatives and produce cleaner electrical current that's safe for sensitive electronics like laptops, CPAP machines, and medical devices. Most solar generators on our list feature pure sine wave inverters with dual AC/DC output, which means they can power virtually any type of device without additional hardware.

Solar input

The maximum wattage figure in a generator's specs represents the maximum electricity it can process from connected solar panels. Some generators feature a Maximum Power Point Tracking (MPPT) charge controller, which optimizes charging efficiency by finding the ideal operating current and voltage for current conditions. MPPT controllers meaningfully improve both capacity utilization and long-term battery health.

Interface and compatibility

Control panel complexity and available connection types vary widely. Some models offer standard wall outlets and little else; others include USB-C, USB-A, and Bluetooth connectivity for mobile app monitoring and control. Wireless capability is particularly convenient for generators used as home backup systems, since it allows you to check status and adjust settings without physically accessing the unit.

Portability

For generators used for camping, outdoor events, or other recreational activities, portability is a real differentiator. Beyond weight, consider wheel size and build quality. Larger, more durable wheels make a meaningful difference when rolling a heavy unit across uneven ground or loading it into a vehicle.

Expandability

Many solar generators support modular expansion by connecting additional battery packs, linking multiple units, or adding solar panel inputs. If your budget doesn't yet reach your ideal setup, buying a model that supports future expansion lets you upgrade over time without starting from scratch.

Buying guide: how to choose the best solar portable generator

There is no one-size-fits-all answer. The right generator will depend on your energy needs, intended use, and budget. Here's a step-by-step framework.

1. Determine your budget

Your budget is your primary constraint. Generally, higher capacity and more advanced technology mean a higher generator cost. Get a realistic sense of what you can comfortably spend, but keep in mind that buying slightly more capacity now is almost always cheaper than replacing an undersized unit later.

2. Figure out your power needs

Whether you're planning recreational use or home backup, you'll need to calculate how much power you actually need. List every device or appliance you want to run, note its wattage draw, and consider whether they'll run simultaneously. If your budget rules out a generator with enough total capacity, prioritize your most essential needs and size to those first.

3. Match your inverter specs

Ensure your chosen generator has a pure sine wave inverter with dual AC/DC capability. This combination lets you safely power sensitive electronics and run the widest possible range of devices. Modified sine wave inverters are significantly riskier for electronics and should generally be avoided.

4. Weigh size vs. portability

Consider whether you'll be moving your generator frequently to campsites or events, or whether it will mostly sit in one place as a home backup. For frequent transport, lighter units with quality wheels are worth prioritizing. For stationary home use, the added weight of higher-capacity models is far less of a factor.

5. Compare solar charging speeds

Input wattage determines how fast your generator recharges via solar panels. This matters more for recreational users and for homes in northern regions with limited winter daylight. Check manufacturer specs for estimated full-charge time at maximum solar input, and compare those figures across models before buying.

6. Consider future expansion

Modular solar generator systems let you grow your setup over time. If your ideal configuration is currently out of budget, buying a unit that supports battery expansion or additional panel connections allows you to upgrade as your situation changes, without starting from scratch.

Find the generator that fits your needs

No single generator fits every home: learn how to choose the best backup generator for your home.

Compare generators
Maintenance tips for solar generators

Solar portable generators don't require nearly as much regular maintenance as gas-powered units, but they do need some ongoing care. Key maintenance tasks include:

Keeping solar panels clean and angled correctly for maximum sun exposure
Storing lithium-ion batteries at moderate temperatures — extreme cold or heat degrades capacity
Monitoring MPPT charge controllers periodically for efficiency anomalies
Testing system functionality, output accuracy, and safety features on a regular schedule
Bottom line: which solar generator is for you?

Any of the five models on this list represents a strong choice, but the right one depends on your specific situation. The EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3 is the best overall option for serious home backup and extended off-grid use. The Goal Zero Yeti PRO 4000 is the pick for disaster preparedness and demanding outdoor work sites. The Anker SOLIX F3800 is ideal for RV owners and anyone needing 240-volt appliance support. The Bluetti AC200L hits the sweet spot for mid-size portability, and the Jackery Explorer 2000 Plus is the most accessible entry point into a modular solar setup on a tighter budget.

Carefully consider how you plan to use your generator, what you need it to power, and what your realistic budget allows. Then use the specs and comparisons in this guide to match those needs to the right model.

 Battery capacity 
Power station battery capacity is measured in Watt Hours (Wh) - or 1 watt of energy used per hour. The higher the number, the more battery capacity the unit has, the longer it lasts without requiring a recharge. To give you an idea of the power a unit has, an iPhone 17 Pro Max has a battery capacity of 20Wh; the cheapest and smallest portable power station in this guide has a capacity of 245Wh.
 Output 
Output measures the total continuous power supply a unit can deliver, and is measured in Watts (W). Small devices like a laptop and coolers tends to need around 60 to 100W of continuous power whereas appliances like fridges can need up to around 800W. So, a large portable power station with a higher output is best for powering large devices, or more devices at once.
 Input 
Portable power stations are usually charged via the mains - it's quick and efficient, especially for higher-capacity units. Many also let you charge the device from the car using a 12V cigarette lighter socket - ideal for those living the van life or in the RV. You can recharge some devices using solar panels, too.
 Solar 
Every portable power station I've selected for this guide have solar charging capabilities for off-grid power supply, but not every unit you can buy does. The solar panels can come bundled with the unit or bought separately. Smaller power stations will have a lower maximum solar input, making them slower to charge.
 UPS 
Uninterrupted Power Supply (UPS) is essential for ensuring reliable and continuous power even during black-outs. If you're using your unit for devices like routers or fridges, it's. Effectively, a UPS-enabled power station will step in during a power outage to continue charging or powering connected devices. Times vary, and while we're talking a matter of milliseconds, if it's a 'mission-critical' device, then select one with a faster switchover time.
 High surge wattage 
 This is especially important if you're using a portable power station on a job-site, as some tools, like circular saws, draw a huge amount of power at once. So, a unit with a high surge wattage (or high surge rating) prevents the machinery from tripping out the unit.
 Size & weight 
"Portable" isn't one size fits all. My team and I have reviewed everything from compact and handheld units to massive power stations that have built in wheels or need a trolley to move them. Depending on how and where you'll be using the unit, you'll want check the dimensions. As you'd expect, the higher the battery capacity, the heavier the power station will be.
 Ports 
Port selection is always worth checking. Portable power stations almost always include USB-C and USB-A ports, as well as mains outlets. However, larger units will usually have a higher number of ports as there's extra space for them, and the unit holds more power to charge more devices. Some go beyond this - for example, DJI's products include an SDC port for charging DJI drones on the go.
 Best portable power stations: FAQs 
 Are portable power stations worth it?
 Yes, but it depends on how often you use it and how many devices you're charging. There are a lot of models on the market, and the best portable power stations can handle everything from charging mobile devices and laptops to powering appliances and even EVs. If your needs are simple, you can pick up a good portable power station for around $200.
If you like going to campsites that have a power hookup they're not worth it as connecting to mains doesn't cost that much compared to a power station. For longer periods off-grid a generator is still, for me, the better option but for short weekend trips where you cannot get a power source these can completely change the weekend for the better if you want to keep using your tech or use electric-powered camping gadgets.
 What is the difference between a portable power station and a generator?
 Generally speaking, a portable power station is charged and outputs electricity. Generators tend to refer to units that use fuel like gasoline to generate energy and power. 
 Both can be used for back-up purposes, and both have different pros and cons. 
 Power stations are quieter, cleaner and more eco-friendly. However, their battery capacity can be low, and if it runs out of charge during a power-cut, you'd best hope it has built-in solar panels to re-charge. 
 Power generators are ideal for running heavy appliances, as they have a higher capacity, and isn't reliant on electricity, making it perfect for a back-up solution. 
 How many years do portable power stations last?
 A portable power station's lifespan depends on usage frequency and battery chemistry, but most last between 5 and 10 years with regular use. Like a phone or laptop battery, its capacity gradually degrades over time until it can no longer hold a full charge.
 THere are several key factors influence a portable power station's longevity: 
 The first is the battery type; models with Lithium Iron Phosphate (LiFePO4) batteries often last up to 10 years (3,000+ full charge cycles), while standard Lithium-ion (NMC) models usually last 3 to 5 years (500 to 1,000 cycles) before capacity drops to 80%. 
 The second and third factors, which we've combines, depends on a station's usage and storage; frequent deep discharges, exposure to extreme temperatures, and storing the unit fully empty accelerate battery degradation all affect its lifespan.
 How many Watt Hours do I need?
 Start by listing every device or appliance you want to power. For anything you'll run continuously — a fridge, a router, a lamp — multiply its wattage by the number of hours you need it running. For devices you'll charge and then use, like a phone or laptop, find the battery capacity in Wh (usually on the device label or manufacturer's website) and multiply that by the number of times you want to charge it.
 Add all those figures together and that's your minimum capacity requirement.
 It's worth adding a 20–30% buffer on top of that figure. Real-world capacity is affected by temperature, battery age, and the startup surge that motors and compressors draw when they first switch on.
 What can you run on a portable power station?
 So long as your portable power station has the right ports and enough capacity, it can run a massive range of devices, including phones, laptops, and desktops. 
 Higher capacity units will also let you power large home appliances and charge electric vehicles. 
 Check which ports your preferred model has, including USB Type-A and Type-C, AC and mains sockets.
 How long can you run a portable power station?
 It all depends on the power station and the device or devices you're charging. As a general rule of thumb, to figure out how long your portable power station can run, divide battery capacity (Wh) by power drawn by the device (W). 
 What is UPS and why do I need it?
 UPS stands for Uninterrupted Power Supply, and it’s a really important feature if you’re powering devices like routers and household appliances like fridges, or working on-site and need reliability. If you experience a power outage, the portable power station will automatically and seamlessly continue charge your devices without dropping the supply. 
 How we test the best portable power stations 
 Our team of expert reviewers have hand-tested a range of outdoor-ready equipment, including the best rugged smartphones , the best rugged laptops , and the best rugged tablets for working out in the field. We've even tested out the best rugged hard drives . So, we know what to look for when it comes to technology for rural locations and hostile environments.
 We test the best portable power stations on volume, weight, battery chemistry, and additional feature sets. Before writing any review, we try to fully understand the unit to describe each device's pros and cons best and accurately compare them. Part of this process is through benchmark tests, part is through daily use, and part is through simulated or real scenarios.
 As the main function of these devices is to be batteries, we test charge and discharge cycles on every unit. First and foremost, this is the most important feature of the portable power stations we test. If they cannot meet our standard here or do not come near what the other portable power stations in this guide are capable of, we will most likely not include them.
 Next, we push the power stations to their limits and beyond. We intentionally exceed the maximum power allowed on each generator, then observe and note the recovery from the over-power protection. This helps us promote safe power stations for you and your family.
 To ensure reliability, these tests are designed to learn the features, the downfalls, and the limits of the power stations tested by our subject matter experts.

 Is a Solar Generator Worth It? 
 What to Consider 
 Power stations (i.e., solar generators) have become increasingly popular because they are easy to run, cost less over time than gas generators , and offer eco-friendly, emission-free operation, especially when paired with a solar panel . Some are small and compact, ideal for off-grid adventures, while larger ones are able to back up critical home circuits during a blackout.
 Unlike fuel-based generators, solar generators can’t create electricity in real time. They’re giant battery packs, not true generators, and need to be recharged using alternating-current (AC) power or solar panels, the latter of which often takes many hours in ideally sunny conditions.
 Despite those distinctions compared to portable generators , there’s nothing more convenient than a power station for charging or running everything you need for day-to-day life—phones and laptops, lights, and even a small appliance or two . Plus, it’s nice to have a device that doesn’t produce carbon emissions and replenishes itself freely from the sun’s rays. Whether you’re seeking a highly portable option or need one that’s heavy-duty enough for extended use, these are the best solar generators we’ve tested and researched to date.

 What to Consider
 Size and Capacity
 Power stations use watts and watt-hours to express size and capacity. Watts (size) refer to how much power it produces. For example, if you need to run a 900-watt microwave, you’ll need a station that outputs at least that much power (ideally more, since factory specs are never exact).
 Meanwhile, watt-hours (capacity) give you an idea of how long devices can be powered continuously, though how much time depends on the amount of power being drawn—watt-hours don’t dictate a set time frame. Higher-powered devices will drain the battery a lot faster than lower-powered ones.
 That may seem confusing, but a simple equation gives you an approximate idea of how it works: total watt-hours (of the generator) ÷ watts (of the device) = hours the power station runs.
 For example, if you had a power station with a 2,048-watt-hour capacity and wanted to run a 750-watt space heater consistently at its highest setting, it would probably run for around 2.5 hours, so long as nothing else is plugged in. But for a refrigerator, whose power draw fluctuates between 10 and 300 watts (depending on how often the compressor turns on), you might be able to run it for nearly 24 hours.
 Keep in mind that manufacturer specs are taken from perfect conditions; in the real world, you’ll likely see slightly less capacity from your power station. If you’re not sure how much power the different devices in your home draw, sometimes it’s written on a label, or you can use a device like a wattmeter .
 Solar Panel Capacity
 Just as a power station has specifications on output size and capacity, solar panels are rated by how many watts they produce for a device after they convert the sun’s rays into electrical current (e.g., 100 watts, 200 watts, etc.). Because real-world conditions are never perfect, it’s not uncommon for panels to only output 50 to 75 percent (or even lower) of their total potential.
 Your panels must also be within the acceptable input range of the power station. For example, connecting a 400-watt solar-panel array to a power station that only accepts 110 watts of solar input can cause an overload and damage the station.
 Portability
 While weight and size don’t directly correlate to the technicalities of power banks, they impact the convenience of each model. Many camping and overlanding setups have limited space, so the more compact models likely have a higher appeal as a result.
 That said, most units weigh at least 10 pounds, and the weight and size increase quickly with greater capacities. Before purchasing, consider where you plan to store the power bank and the space in your vehicle or camper where it will live while you’re on the road. If you plan to use this power bank solely as a home backup option, portability will matter less, but consider how much effort it will take to move it around within your home or in your outdoor space.
 David Dritsas Even portable solar panels can take up a lot of space when fully unfolded, and even on a perfectly sunny day, won’t achieve their advertised potential. For example, this 200-watt panel from Goal Zero only averaged about 130 watts of converted power (which is not bad).
 FAQs
 What are your priorities when choosing a solar-powered generator? 
 I am a low-maintenance camper, and most of my background is in lightweight backcountry travel. That means I prioritize space-saving and ease-of-use, so my go-to power banks have between 250 and 600 watt-hours, and weigh less than 15 pounds.
 This is perfect for a weekend trip, with the on-the-go (car or solar) charging capabilities to put my mind at ease for longer trips. Mostly, I’m charging small items, so one charge lasts a long time. However, plenty of people in the van-life and remote-work world are powering their RVs and vans, and relying on multiple laptop charges. For that, I’d recommend one of the larger units.
 What can a solar-powered generator charge and power? 
 A solar-powered generator charges and runs almost anything that requires power—it just depends on the capacity. These generators can charge power tools in the shop, laptops for remote work, and personal devices like Bluetooth headphones and speakers .
 A solar-powered generator with a higher power capacity can even power household appliances in the event of a power outage. And the fact that these are solar-compatible means you aren’t reliant on the electrical grid to recharge them.
 What is the best way to charge a power station? 
 Every unit on our list has multiple charging options, including wall (AC outlet), car (12-volt), and solar. Each input method charges your unit at a different speed, and solar also depends on the conditions. AC power is the fastest, followed by 12-volt, and then by solar (though a larger solar array could potentially be faster than 12-volt).
 I try to charge up my power banks whenever I can, so I’m never caught off guard trying to leave on a trip with a dying power bank. If this happens (which it has), I’ll charge it in my vehicle’s 12-volt port while I’m driving, though this is often slower than solar or a wall unit.
 Solar power is the most sustainable and typically fastest way to power these—just be sure you have enough wattage in the solar panels to make it effective. I recommend keeping the generator stored with at least an 80 percent charge, and unplugging it once it’s fully charged—keeping it plugged in longer than necessary degrades the battery.
 Most units will have a simple readout display showing the remaining battery charge, and it’s a good practice not to allow your battery pack to get below 20 percent.

 Best Solar Generator FAQ
 What is the best solar generator? 
 The EcoFlow Delta Pro 3 is our best overall solar generator of 2026, for its 4,096 Wh capacity, 4,000W output, 240V support and 2,600W of solar input. For most people the Jackery Explorer 1000 V2 is the better buy: 1,070 Wh at 23 lb covers a fridge overnight and still goes camping.
 What is the top-rated solar generator? 
 In our ratings, the EcoFlow Delta Pro 3 scores highest at 95/100. Our reviews hub ranks every model we rate in a sortable chart.
 What is the best budget solar generator? 
 The EcoFlow River 3 Plus won our formula-scored Best Budget 2026 award: 286 Wh with a 600W AC outlet, 220W solar input, a sub-10 ms UPS mode and an optional extra battery.
 What size solar generator do I need? 
 About 300 Wh for phones, laptops and a CPAP night; about 1,000 Wh for a fridge overnight; 2,000 Wh or more for a multi-day outage; and 3,000 to 5,000 Wh for essential home circuits through a transfer switch.
 Are solar generators worth it? 
 For outage backup, camping and RV use, usually yes: they are silent, fume-free and safe indoors, with no fuel to store. A gas generator is cheaper per kilowatt-hour of runtime but must run outdoors because of carbon monoxide.
 How long do solar generators last? 
 The LiFePO4 batteries in every pick here are designed for thousands of charge cycles, so most owners will replace the unit for other reasons before the battery wears out. Storage habits matter: keep it partly charged and top it up every few months.
 Which solar generator brand is best? 
 No single brand wins every category. Jackery leads on portable and camping picks, EcoFlow on whole-home and budget, Anker SOLIX on fast charging and emergencies, Bluetti on value, and Pecron on high-capacity value.
 When is the best time to buy a solar generator? 
 The November window, Black Friday through Cyber Monday, has historically produced the year's deepest pricing on these models. Prime Big Deal Days in October has historically been the other strong window.
